messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Margaret, a 61-year-old policy analyst, had spent decades reviewing environmental regulations, but nothing prepared her for the moment a chemical fire erupted in the storage room beneath her office. She was alone in a conference room when the smoke alarm sounded, and by the time she reached the stairwell, acrid fumes had already filled the corridor. She crouched on the floor, coughing, unable to see the exit, certain she was about to pass out. Firefighters pulled her out after twenty minutes, but the memory of that helpless, gasping panic never left her.

In the months that followed, Margaret found herself avoiding the television news—any report of a factory fire or chemical spill made her chest tighten. She also stopped watching documentaries about industrial accidents, though she had once found them professionally interesting. At work, she began scanning every room she entered for exits. When she attended meetings, she always chose a seat with her back to a wall and a clear path to the door. She told herself it was just common sense, but she knew it was more than that.

The smells were the worst. A whiff of smoke from a colleague’s cigarette outside the building could send her heart racing, and she would immediately think, *I can’t trust myself to stay calm*. That thought—*I can’t rely on myself*—had taken root during the fire, when she had frozen instead of finding the exit. Now, whenever she caught a burnt smell—from a toaster in the break room or a passing car—the same self-doubt surged back: *I’ll never be able to feel normal emotions again.* That negative appraisal, in turn, made her even more vigilant. She would scan the room for threats, her body already tense, which only confirmed her belief that she was fundamentally unsafe in her own skin.

The cycle tightened. One day, Margaret smelled alcohol—hand sanitizer from a dispenser in the hallway—and her stomach dropped. The odor triggered a flash of the chemical fumes, and the thought came unbidden: *I can’t rely on myself to get out of here.* She immediately began scanning for exits, her heart pounding, and she chose a seat near the stairwell for the rest of the afternoon. Later, she spent an hour ruminating about how she could have prevented the fire—if she had checked the storage room herself, if she had insisted on a better evacuation plan. That rumination, a Maladaptive Strategy she had developed, only deepened her self-doubt. She told herself she had failed once, so she would fail again.

Margaret’s checking of her surroundings became constant. She would re-scan rooms she had already entered, looking for anything out of place. Her physical reactivity—the racing heart, the sweating—when she smelled smoke or burnt odors made her believe even more strongly that she had lost control of her emotions. And that belief heightened her threat monitoring: the more she thought she couldn’t trust herself, the more she searched for danger. The searches, in turn, brought her into contact with triggers she might otherwise have missed, like the faint alcohol smell from cleaning supplies in the hallway, which then restarted the whole sequence.

As a policy analyst, Margaret’s job required meetings and public hearings, but she now arrived early to claim a “safe seat” and avoided the cafeteria, where a faint burnt toast smell sometimes lingered. She had stopped attending professional development seminars because they might include video footage of industrial accidents. Her husband noticed she had become withdrawn, refusing invitations to dinner parties where someone might grill with charcoal. She worried she was letting everyone down, and that worry—*I can’t do the right thing*—made her avoid even friendly gatherings.

What finally brought Margaret to seek help was a morning when she could not bring herself to enter her own kitchen because she thought she smelled gas. There was no leak; it was just the smell of a neighbor’s barbecue drifting in. She stood in the hallway, trembling, and realized she was trapped in a cycle she could not break on her own. She came to therapy afraid that she would never feel normal again, but she was also quietly hoping that maybe, this time, she could learn to trust herself.
